newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain outraged as ETA kidnap victim nears death.
newsitem.headline: Spain outraged as ETA kidnap victim nears death.

text.p: Basque separatists who kidnapped a Spanish politician have shot their victim in the head, leaving him close to death, and more than a million people took to the streets to express their outrage.

Doctors said Miguel Angel Blanco, a 29-year-old Basque town councillor, showed signs of "irreversible" brain damage after his ETA kidnappers shot him on Saturday and was unlikely to survive for long. He had two bullets lodged in his brain and was in a deep coma.

In a series of marches and rallies, more than a million Spaniards turned out across the nation in a show of solidarity with Blanco and opposition to ETA, which has killed some 800 people in a nearly 30-year fight for independence.

In the Basque capital Bilbao alone, half a million Spaniards led by Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar demonstrated against the guerrilla action. Officials said it was the biggest protest rally against ETA separatist rebels in history.
Leading politicians denounced ETA's action and urged calm.
"The government expresses its strongest condemnation against this barbarity," chief government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez told reporters.
After the shooting, unknown attackers firebombed the seat of ETA's political wing Herri Batasuna in Blanco's hometown Ermua, but the fire was put out quickly and there was little damage.

Organisers of Pamplona's world-famous running of the bulls suspended the festival on Saturday in support of Blanco. It was the first such interruption since 1978 when it was cancelled after clashes with Basque nationalist demonstrators.
A Vatican spokesman told Spanish state radio that Pope John Paul II was praying for Blanco and his family.

Basque ETA rebels kidnapped Blanco on Thursday and threatened to kill him at 4 p.m. (1400 GMT) on Saturday if the government did not change its policy on rebel prisoners. The goverment called it blackmail and rejected the demands.
A hunter who heard a shot in a wooded area near the northern Basque coastal city of San Sebastian found Blanco bleeding and with his hands tied. He saw a man running from the scene.
Police later found a car they believed was used as a getaway vehicle by the kidnappers. They thought it contained a bomb, but no explosives were found.

There was also confusion at first about whether Blanco had been killed or not. When he was rushed to hospital, a duty judge who went there reported Blanco was dead. Hospital officials later said he was alive and in a coma.

ETA kidnapped Blanco, a low-ranking member of Aznar's ruling Popular Party apparently targeted because he had no bodyguards, and said they would kill him unless the government transferred some 500 ETA inmates to prisons in the Basque country.
The kidnapping and death threat caused outrage across Spain, which had just been celebrating the release of two other ETA hostages last week.
Even nationalist politicians in the region who support the separatist cause but oppose violence turned out for the protest in Bilbao and called on ETA to release Blanco.

"They (ETA) have to know we cannot live with this barbarity any longer. If they carry out this threat, the Basque people will never, never forgive them," Basque interior counsellor Juan Maria Atutxa told state television in Bilbao.

Aznar headed the protest march in Bilbao marching alongside his wife and fierce Basque nationalist leader Jose Antonio Ardanza. They carried a yellow banner at the front that said "Peace Now and Forever" in the Basque language.
After news of the attack, a visibally furious Ardanza blasted ETA and, more unusally for the nationalist leader, its political wing Herri Batasuna.

"It's time for them to be denounced publicly. Herri Batasuna (HB), you always want to be presented as victims in this society but you are the executioners," Ardanza told a news conference. "Enough already, not just ETA but also HB."
He said all Basque political parties except HB would meet on Sunday to discuss a response, while Madrid called a meeting on Monday of the multi-party anti-terrorist group.
A former Herri Batasuna counsellor and several former members of ETA condemned the shooting as senseless violence.
"I never though ETA would carry out this attack," Jose Egia, formerly of HB, said. "This will cause a great loss of votes."

ETA is seeking an independent Basque state encompassing parts of northern Spain and southern France. The rebels have set deadlines to execute kidnap victims twice before, in 1981 and 1983, and in both cases the hostages were killed.
